L9: # Register your interest in our dog cancer trial
L10: 
L11: We are recruiting dogs with mast cell cancer in Australia for an investigational trial of personalised mRNA cancer vaccines. Register your interest and share a few details about your dog. Our team will contact you about further screening.
L12: 
L13: 【5†Register your interest  →】 【8†See how it works  →】
L14: 
L15: Why we are running this trial
L16: ## From Rosie’s story to a future for more dogs.
L17: 
L18: 【9†Image: Rosie】
L19: 
L20: Rosie
L21: 
L22: The first dog treated with a personalised neoantigen vaccine.
L23: 
L24: It began with Rosie. Her experience with a personalised neoantigen vaccine encouraged Paul to explore how this approach could one day be made available to every dog with cancer.
L25: Before an approach like this can become broadly available, we must study it carefully and support it by evidence for review by the relevant veterinary regulators. This clinical trial is an important step in that process, helping us learn from participating dogs and understand the vaccine more fully.
L26: 
L27: 【2†Read Rosie’s personalised mRNA cancer-vaccine story  →】
L28: 
L29: Who can register
L30: ## If your dog has cancer and is currently in Australia, you’re welcome to register your interest. Our team will check whether your dog may be eligible for this trial.
L31: 
L32: 【5†Register your interest  →】
L33: 
L34: About the trial
L35: 
L36: ## What this trial is looking at
L37: 
L38: The trial will investigate a personalised mRNA vaccine approach for dogs with mast cell cancer. Tell us about your dog and our team will help determine whether they may be eligible for screening.
L39: 
L40: 【10†Image】
L41: ### Who can register
L42: 
L43: Dogs diagnosed with mast cell cancer who are based in, or able to travel within, Australia.
L44: 
L45: Every case is reviewed individually
L46: 
L47: 【11†Image】
L48: 
L49: ### The trial approach
L50: 
L51: A therapeutic mRNA vaccine designed from each dog’s own tumour and blood samples, intended to work alongside—not replace—existing care.
L52: 
L53: Personalised to each dog
L54: 
L55: 【12†Image】
L56: ### What screening involves
L57: 
L58: We help coordinate records, screening, sample logistics and updates, working with the trial team and your treating veterinarian.
L59: 
L60: A named team stays in touch
L61: 
L62: Trial registration and screening
L63: 
L64: ## How to register your interest.
L65: 
L66: You don’t need to have every record ready before registering your interest. Start with what you know and we’ll help with the rest.
L67: 
L68: 01
L69: ### Register your interest
L70: 
L71: Complete a short form with basic details about your dog, their mast cell cancer diagnosis and where you live.
L72: 
L73: 02
L74: 
L75: ### We get in touch
L76: 
L77: A Gamgee coordinator will contact you, answer practical questions and—with your permission—help gather relevant records from your vet.
L78: 
L79: 03

L40: # UQ launches vaccine trial for dogs with bone cancer
L41: 
L42: 21 July 2023
L43: 
L44: 【23†Image: a grey and black dog in a blue jumper lies on a mattress】
L45: 
L46: Barney, owned by Professor Allavena, was given an early version of the vaccine when diagnosed with an aggressive bone cancer and 10 months later is alive and well.
L47: 
L48: University of Queensland veterinary researchers are recruiting pet dogs diagnosed with cancer to test an experimental vaccine.
L49: The clinical research trial is for dogs recently diagnosed with canine appendicular osteosarcoma, a common bone tumour that affects 10,000 dogs a year globally.
L50: 
L51: 【24†Dr Abhilasha Dadhich†veterinary-science.uq.edu.au】 from UQ’s 【25†School of Veterinary Science†veterinary-science.uq.edu.au】 said researchers will assess two vaccine formulations.
L52: 
L53: “These treatments aim to stimulate a dog’s immune system to fight the spread of cancerous cells to other tissues of the body,” Dr Dadhich said.
L54: “We’re essentially ‘waking up’ the dog’s immune system to fight the cancer.
L55: 
L56: “This has real potential to enhance the life expectancy of the pets in the trial.”
L57: 
L58: To be eligible, dogs need to have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma of long bones of the limbs with no evidence of metastasis, or cancer spread, based on a physical exam and radiographs.
L59: 
L60: Dogs can be any breed but must be proceeding to surgery to treat their cancer.
L61: “If the dog meets these parameters, their owner will simply need to sign an informed consent document after the trial has been explained,” Dr Dadhich said.
L62: 
L63: “The veterinary clinic will then collect blood and cancerous bone tissue from the dog at the time of surgery.
L64: 
L65: “Our prepared treatment is provided for free, administered to the dog in two doses.
L66: 
L67: “The first vaccine dose will be given within two weeks of their surgery and the second dose as a booster three weeks later.

L5: ## Benefits and Participation
L6: 
L7:   * Owners are financially responsible for the initial exam and screening tests to determine eligibility.
L8:   * Following the initial exam and screening, the remainder of this trial is funded for up to 2 months of treatment including tumor biopsy, recheck exams, bloodwork, and chemotherapy.
L9:   * Recheck visits for blood draws and monitoring are required and covered by the study.
L10: ## Inclusion Criteria
L11: 
L12:   * Diagnosis of mammary carcinoma, melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, histiocytic sarcoma, or apocrine anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA)
L13:   * Measurable tumor on physical exam
L14:   * Prior cancer treatment is allowed, but dogs must have cancer progression at the time of enrollment
L15:   * Pet must be otherwise healthy
L16: ## Clinical Trial Background
L17: 
L18:   * Cancer is ranked as the top cause of death in dogs.
L19:   * New anti-cancer therapies are desperately needed.
L20:   * Palbociclib is an oral chemotherapy drug used in various human cancers.
L21:   * Palbociclib has the potential to treat many canine cancers, however, the ideal dose has yet to be established in dogs.

L29: # Devoted to the Fight Against Canine Cancer
L30: 
L31: We seek to break the barriers of traditional cancer treatment. Through collaboration with colleagues and research scientists, we want to offer the most effective cancer treatment for canine B cell lymphoma.
L32: ## Why We Do It
L33: 
L34: Canine B cell lymphoma is a very prevalent cancer in dogs of all breeds. It behaves much like non-Hodgkin lymphoma in humans and much of the research has taken place with dogs. Aurelius Biotherapeutics is utilizing this information and applying it to canine lymphoma treatment.
L35: ## Canine Lymphoma Treatment
L36: 
L37: For the past decade, our team has concentrated on the treatment of canine B cell lymphoma using adoptive transfer of T cells, commonly referred to as ACT. Our sole focus is to deliver safe and effective adoptive T cell immunotherapy in the fight against cancer. By using the patients own T cells, we can enhance the immune system so it can recognize and fight the cancer cells more effectively.
L38: ## What is T cell Therapy?
L39: 
L40: Cells from the patient's own immune system, T lymphocytes, are collected, cultured and activated to be tumor-cell specific. Once their numbers are maximally expanded, they are infused back in to the patient.  By recruiting the immune system we hope to provide another way to fight the cancer cells
L41: 
L42: 【12†Image: process of t cell therapy in treating lymphoma in dogs】
L43: ## T Cell Therapies
L44: Lately, immunotherapy treatment that uses the patients’ immune cells has grown in importance.  Adoptive transfer of T cells provides a novel approach in the fight against cancer. T cells are removed from the blood stream and those cells that are specifically fighting the cancer are selected and expanded. Recently, Novartis has won FDA approval for a unique form of T cell therapy using CAR T therapy.
L45: CAR T cell therapy refers to a process using the patients’ T cells which are selected and genetically modified to identify the tumor antigen more effectively. Aurelius Biotherapeutics uses another type of immunotherapy that doesn't genetically modify the T cells. By growing the lymphocytes with antigens from the tumor, we reactivate the T cells in their fight against the cancer cells.

L5: # Gold Nanoparticles - Active Enrollment
L6: 
L7: We are conducting a trial for utilizing gold nanoparticles paired with infrared laser heat. Eligible patients have to have superficial tumors. We are treating the following types:
L8: 
L9: 【4†Image†images.squarespace-cdn.com】
L10: 
L11:   * Dogs with large mast cell tumors (>2 cm)
L12: 
L13:   * Dogs with soft tissue sarcomas (<2cm in diameter)
L14: 
L15:   * Dogs with oral melanoma (2-3cm diameter)
L16: 
L17:   * Dogs with cutaneous or footpad melanoma (<2cm)
L18:   * Cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma not involving the bone
L19: 
L20:   * Cats with other cutaneous tumors like Mast cell tumors, Sarcomas or Carcinomas
L21: 
L22: This clinical trial utilizes gold nanoparticles in a gross disease setting.
L23: Gold Nanoparticles are inert and are given IV to the patient and after a period of time the patient comes back to have the tumor heated with a laser. As the tumor vasculature is heated through the external near infrared spectrum of light, the gold nanoparticles are excited, the laser energy is converted to heat and the tumor vasculature is disrupted killing the tumor from the inside out.
L24: Smaller tumors typically need only the 1 session of heat but larger tumors may need more than 1 session of heat (average 2-3 for sarcomas).
L25: 
L26: THE TRIAL IS NOW ENROLLING PATIENTS!
L27: 
L28: If you have a potential case to discuss, have a patient with a tumor in a bad location for surgery or if you would like to learn more, please contact us at 425-697-2272 for more information.
L29: # Gilvetmab paired with EGFR for Histo diagnosed Hemangiosarcoma - CLOSED
L30: 
L31: 
L32: 
L33: The current clinical trial for EGFR vaccination with Yale has been granted the rights to add Gilvetmab for these patients through a MERCK Product Grant Support. These patients received Gilvetmab paired with Carboplatin and EGFR. We will now be looking at dogs with Carboplatin and EGFR as the comparison arm.
L34: #  Paclitaxel for K9 Hemangiosarcoma - CLOSED
L35: 
L36: BARC was enrolling patients in a clinical trial for a unique chemotherapy agent for splenic hemangiosarcoma patients but we have reached the enrollment goal and the trial is now closed. The company that produces Paclitaxel will be evaluating the results in hopes to bring the drug to market.
L37: 
L38: Trial Status: CLOSED FOR DATA REVIEW
L39: # Paclitaxel for Feline Tumors - CLOSED
L40: 
L41: BARC was enrolling Feline patients in a clinical trial for Paclitaxel in a variety of tumor types. The company that produces Paclitaxel will be evaluating the results in hopes to bring the drug to market.

L16: 
L17:   * Dogs with cutaneous or footpad melanoma (<2cm)
L18:   * Cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma not involving the bone
L19: 
L20:   * Cats with other cutaneous tumors like Mast cell tumors, Sarcomas or Carcinomas
L21: 
L22: This clinical trial utilizes gold nanoparticles in a gross disease setting.
L23: Gold Nanoparticles are inert and are given IV to the patient and after a period of time the patient comes back to have the tumor heated with a laser. As the tumor vasculature is heated through the external near infrared spectrum of light, the gold nanoparticles are excited, the laser energy is converted to heat and the tumor vasculature is disrupted killing the tumor from the inside out.
L24: Smaller tumors typically need only the 1 session of heat but larger tumors may need more than 1 session of heat (average 2-3 for sarcomas).
L25: 
L26: THE TRIAL IS NOW ENROLLING PATIENTS!
L27: 
L28: If you have a potential case to discuss, have a patient with a tumor in a bad location for surgery or if you would like to learn more, please contact us at 425-697-2272 for more information.

L6: # Clinical Study for Cats with Mammary Cancer - Information for owners
L7: 
L8: ##
L9: 
L10: ## The care your cat will receive
L11: ### Standard surgical care
L12: 
L13: Your cat will undergo routine tumour removal, just like any cat receiving mammary gland surgery at our Veterinary Teaching Hospital.
L14: 
L15: ### Innovative therapy
L16: 
L17: In addition to standard treatment, your cat will receive the investigational therapy (GCN2-IN-6) that will need to be administered orally before and after the surgery.
L18: ### Close monitoring
L19: 
L20: Apart from you as an owner, veterinary specialists will follow your cat throughout the study to ensure their comfort, safety, and well-being.
L21: Preclinical studies at the Small Animal Department demonstrated that this therapy is well-tolerated by cats, with little to no side effects nor with any relevant changes in any blood parameter.
L22: 
L23: ## Benefits and Impact
L24: ### Potential benefit for your cat
L25: 
L26: Participation may help to lower the risk of tumour recurrence and/or tumour spread (metastasis).
L27: The novel drug will be supplied without any additional cost.
L28: 
L29: ### Advancing feline care
L30: 
L31: Your cat’s involvement contributes valuable information toward developing new cancer treatments to increase the life expectancy for cats.
L32: ### Helping humans too
L33: 
L34: The insights gained from this study in cats could pave the way to initiate clinical trials in people with aggressive breast cancers, including TNBC.
L35: 
L36: ## Your Contribution Makes a Difference
L37: 
L38: Without caring owners like you, advancing new treatments to improve the health and lifespan of pets wouldn’t be possible. By participating, you are making a meaningful contribution to advancements in veterinary medicine and helping shape better care for cats, today and in the future.
L39: ### Voluntary participation
L40: 
L41: Participation in this clinical study is completely voluntary. In consultation with the responsible researchers, you may withdraw your cat at any time, without affecting future veterinary care.
L42: 
L43: ### Where the study takes place
L44: 
L45: The study will be conducted at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital of Ghent University, Salisburylaan 133, B-9820 Merelbeke-Melle.
L46: ### Contact information
L47: 
L48: For further information concerning this study, please do not hesitate to contact veterinarian A. Krupa  (adriana.krupa@ugent.be) or Prof. H. de Rooster (hilde.derooster@ugent.be) or contact the reception of the Veterinary Teaching Hospital (+32 9 264 77 00).
